title: Delta Table Engineering & Optimization
subtitle: Writes, overwrite semantics, schemas and physical layout in production
mantra: Write explicitly (create, append, replace a slice), evolve schemas locally, and keep files few, big and clustered on what you filter.
objectives: You can create Delta tables with CREATE, CREATE OR REPLACE, CTAS, LIKE and the PySpark writeTo()/saveAsTable() APIs.
You can choose between append, full overwrite, REPLACE WHERE and REPLACE USING, and design idempotent writes.
You can explain schema enforcement, per-write evolution (mergeSchema / WITH SCHEMA EVOLUTION), overwriteSchema and type widening.
You can inspect tables with DESCRIBE TABLE / DETAIL / HISTORY and diagnose small files and failed data skipping.
You can apply OPTIMIZE, liquid clustering (CLUSTER BY, OPTIMIZE FULL) and predictive optimization correctly.
You can run the 5 Delta debugging workflows and follow the 13 best practices.

sections.title: Creating Delta Tables in SQL
sections.hook: CREATE vs CREATE OR REPLACE is the difference between 'safe' and 'I just wiped prod'.

blocks.text: Phase 2 goal: move from 'I understand Delta internals' to '**I can use Delta correctly in production**' — syntax, APIs, patterns, optimization.

PHASE 2 — DELTA LAKE IN PRACTICE
1. Table creation + writes
2. UPDATE / DELETE / MERGE
3. Write modes + overwrite semantics
4. Schema enforcement / evolution / type widening
5. History / time travel / restore / vacuum
6. Physical optimization: small files, OPTIMIZE,
   data skipping, file stats, deletion vectors,
   liquid clustering, predictive optimization
blocks.caption: Roadmap (internals of DML/MERGE/history live in Chapter 5)

blocks.text: In Databricks, tables are **Delta by default** unless you ask for another format. Databricks recommends **Unity Catalog managed Delta tables** for most workloads.

blocks.code:
CREATE TABLE ecommerce.bronze.orders_raw (
  order_id    BIGINT,
  customer_id BIGINT,
  amount      DECIMAL(10,2),
  status      STRING,
  order_ts    TIMESTAMP
);            -- Delta by default
blocks.caption: Project: catalog ecommerce · schema bronze · table orders_raw

blocks.text: `USING DELTA` is optional today, but useful when teaching or when you want to be **absolutely explicit**.

blocks.title: CREATE OR REPLACE in production
blocks.text: Handy in development, dangerous in production if not used consciously: it replaces the existing table definition and its current state. (On Delta the replace is a new version, so history survives — but downstream consumers instantly see the new state.)
**CTAS — CREATE TABLE AS SELECT.** You don't declare a schema; it is **derived from the query**. Databricks uses this pattern even in its official Delta tutorials.

blocks.code:
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE ecommerce.silver.orders AS
SELECT
  CAST(order_id AS BIGINT)       AS order_id,
  customer_id,
  CAST(amount AS DECIMAL(10,2))  AS amount,
  UPPER(status)                  AS status,
  order_ts
FROM ecommerce.bronze.orders_raw;
blocks.caption: CTAS: Bronze → Silver with casts and cleanup

blocks.text: **CREATE TABLE LIKE** copies the table **definition/metadata, not the data** — an empty table with the same structure.

blocks.code:
CREATE TABLE ecommerce.silver.orders_test
LIKE ecommerce.silver.orders;

blocks.label: Exercise 1 — think first: you want an empty table with the same schema as `prod.silver.customers`, no data. What do you write?
blocks.text: `CREATE TABLE dev.silver.customers LIKE prod.silver.customers;`

sections.title: Creating & Writing from PySpark
sections.hook: Two writer APIs, one positional trap: know writeTo(), saveAsTable() and why insertInto() bites.

blocks.text: The modern recommended API is **DataFrameWriterV2**: `df.writeTo(...)`.

blocks.code:
df.writeTo("ecommerce.bronze.orders_raw").create()
df.writeTo("ecommerce.bronze.orders_raw").createOrReplace()
df.writeTo("ecommerce.silver.orders").append()

(df.writeTo("ecommerce.bronze.orders_raw")
   .using("delta")
   .createOrReplace())
blocks.caption: writeTo() — V2 API

blocks.text: The classic API is still everywhere: `df.write…saveAsTable(...)`.

blocks.code:
df.write.saveAsTable("ecommerce.bronze.orders_raw")

(df.write
   .mode("overwrite")
   .saveAsTable("ecommerce.bronze.orders_raw"))
blocks.caption: saveAsTable() — classic DataFrameWriter

items.title: saveAsTable() (classic)
points: You'll see it in most existing code

blocks.title: Know both
blocks.text: For new code prefer `writeTo()` where practical — but read and maintain `saveAsTable()` code fluently.
**insertInto() — important trap.** `df.write.insertInto("ecommerce.silver.orders")` requires a compatible schema, but it matches columns **by position, not by name**.

target:     id BIGINT | name STRING
DataFrame:  name      | id
              │          │
insertInto -> col1 -> id,  col2 -> name   (positional!)
if types can be coerced -> silently WRONG mapping

blocks.label: Exercise 2 — think first: target (id BIGINT, name STRING), DataFrame columns (name, id). Which API is more dangerous?
blocks.text: `insertInto(...)` — it uses **position-based** resolution, so `name` lands in `id` (or fails only if the cast is impossible). Name-based APIs (`saveAsTable` append, `writeTo().append()`) avoid this.

blocks.title: Positional resolution
blocks.text: If types allow coercion, `insertInto` can write values into the wrong columns without any error. Reorder with `df.select(target_cols)` or use a name-based API.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when values land in the wrong columns
questions: Did I write with insertInto (positional) instead of a name-based API?
Does the DataFrame column order match the target column order?
Could the types be coerced silently (e.g. numbers into strings)?
Which version introduced the bad rows, so I can RESTORE or fix them?

sections.title: INSERT, INSERT OVERWRITE & TRUNCATE
sections.hook: INTO adds, OVERWRITE replaces, TRUNCATE empties, DROP deletes the object — four verbs, four outcomes.

blocks.caption: INSERT INTO = add rows

blocks.text: **INSERT INTO** is **additive**: it adds rows and never replaces existing ones (the docs say so explicitly).

blocks.code:
INSERT INTO ecommerce.silver.orders
SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount, status, order_ts
FROM ecommerce.bronze.orders_raw
WHERE ingestion_date = current_date();
blocks.caption: INSERT INTO … SELECT — the everyday batch ETL pattern

blocks.text: **INSERT OVERWRITE** does not append: it **overwrites the target scope**. Without a partition/predicate restriction it can replace the **entire** table contents.

blocks.code:
INSERT OVERWRITE TABLE ecommerce.silver.orders
SELECT * FROM staging.orders;

blocks.text:
INSERT INTO       = additive    (existing + new)
INSERT OVERWRITE  = replacement (target scope := new)
**TRUNCATE TABLE** empties a table: schema and table object remain, rows are removed.

blocks.code: TRUNCATE TABLE ecommerce.bronze.orders_raw;

blocks.title: INTO vs OVERWRITE
blocks.text: Q: difference between INSERT INTO and INSERT OVERWRITE? A: INTO **adds** rows; OVERWRITE **replaces the target scope**.

sections.title: Append vs Overwrite & Idempotency
sections.hook: A retry should never double your revenue — design writes that are safe to run twice.

blocks.code:
df.write.mode("append").saveAsTable("ecommerce.silver.orders")
df.writeTo("ecommerce.silver.orders").append()
blocks.caption: append: existing rows + new rows

blocks.code: df.write.mode("overwrite").saveAsTable("ecommerce.silver.orders")
blocks.caption: overwrite: can replace the WHOLE table

head: Mode
Good when…
rows: Data are **genuinely new**, no overlap with existing rows
The target should **exactly equal** this new DataFrame
blocks.caption: Daily file 2026-09-27 orders: which mode?

blocks.title: The overwrite trap
blocks.text: Table holds **3 years** of data. Your DataFrame holds **only yesterday**. `df.write.mode("overwrite").saveAsTable(...)` → the other 3 years vanish from the logical state. One of the most classic production mistakes.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when a table suddenly lost most of its rows after a write
questions: Was the last write mode overwrite (DESCRIBE HISTORY → operationParameters)?
Did the DataFrame contain only a subset (e.g. only yesterday)?
Which version was the last good one, and are its files still within retention?
Should this write have been append, MERGE or REPLACE WHERE instead?

blocks.label: Think first: when exactly is a full overwrite dangerous?
blocks.text: When the DataFrame contains only a **subset** of what the table should contain.
**Idempotent** = running the same operation a second time with the same input does **not change** the final state again. Critical when a job **retries**.

source: id=5, status='PAID'
MERGE run 1: updates id=5 -> PAID
MERGE run 2: updates id=5 -> PAID   (same final state)
=> idempotent

blocks.code:
UPDATE orders
SET amount = amount + 10
WHERE id = 5;
-- run twice: +10, +10  => +20 total  => NOT idempotent

items.title: Idempotent
points: MERGE that sets values from source (`t.status = s.status`)
Full overwrite with the same complete DataFrame
REPLACE WHERE for one date with the same data

items.title: Not idempotent
points: Blind append of the same batch twice (duplicates)

blocks.title: Use MERGE for idempotent upserts
blocks.text: MERGE that **sets** target values from a deduplicated source converges to the same state on every retry.

sections.title: Selective Overwrite: REPLACE WHERE & REPLACE USING
sections.hook: Replace exactly one day (or one country) and leave everything else untouched.

blocks.text: You want to replace only `date = 2026-09-27`. Today there are better options than the legacy `partitionOverwriteMode`: Databricks recommends **REPLACE WHERE** or **REPLACE USING** for new workloads.

blocks.caption: REPLACE WHERE: explicit predicate

blocks.text:
replace rows matching the predicate
leave everything else untouched
REPLACE WHERE is supported on **all compute types**.

blocks.caption: REPLACE USING: dynamic overwrite by key columns

blocks.text: **REPLACE USING** replaces target rows whose values in the listed key columns match those in the **incoming** dataset. It's the recommended replacement for legacy dynamic partition overwrite. (The source also lists `REPLACE ON` as a further per-use-case variant.)

blocks.code:
(df.write
   .mode("overwrite")
   .option("partitionOverwriteMode", "dynamic")
   .saveAsTable("ecommerce.silver.orders"))
blocks.caption: Legacy: dynamic partition overwrite

blocks.title: Legacy
blocks.text: `partitionOverwriteMode = dynamic` is still supported in some contexts but is legacy, not preferred for new workloads, and has compute limitations.

blocks.title: Dynamic overwrite with a stray key
blocks.text: Incoming data meant for `2026-09-27` accidentally contains one row with `order_date = 2024-01-01`. Dynamic overwrite (and REPLACE USING) will replace the **whole 2024-01-01 slice** with that single row. Always **validate the incoming key/partition domain** before writing.

items.title: REPLACE WHERE
points: Stray rows outside the predicate → write fails instead of silently replacing

blocks.label: Exercise 4 — think first: replace only `country='GR'`, keep DE/FR unchanged. Better than full overwrite?
blocks.text: Selective overwrite: `INSERT INTO t REPLACE WHERE country = 'GR' SELECT …`.

blocks.title: Ask yourself before any overwrite
questions: Does my DataFrame contain the whole table, or only a subset?
Which slice (date/country) am I really trying to replace?
Have I validated the distinct key values in the incoming data?
Would REPLACE WHERE with an explicit predicate be safer here?

sections.title: Schema Enforcement & Safe Casting
sections.hook: Schema enforcement is a seatbelt, not a nuisance — it stops bad producers before the CEO dashboard.

blocks.text: Target has `id BIGINT, amount DECIMAL(10,2)`. A DataFrame arrives with `amount STRUCT<foo:INT>`. Default expectation: **the write fails**.

blocks.caption: What schema enforcement prevents

blocks.text: Delta performs **schema validation on write**, using the schema stored in the transaction-log metadata.

items: Columns must exist in the target
Types must match or be **safely castable**

head: Target
Incoming
Result
rows: Fails unless evolution is allowed (next section)

blocks.title: Enforcement vs evolution
blocks.text: **Enforcement** rejects incompatible data. **Evolution** allows specific, controlled schema changes.

blocks.title: Best practice
blocks.text: Use schema enforcement as **protection**, not as a nuisance to disable.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when a write fails with a schema mismatch
questions: What does DESCRIBE TABLE say vs df.printSchema()?
Is it a new column, a different type, or a renamed column?
Is the change intentional evolution — or a bug in the source?
If intentional: can I evolve explicitly and locally (mergeSchema / WITH SCHEMA EVOLUTION / ALTER TABLE)?

sections.title: Schema Evolution: mergeSchema, autoMerge, overwriteSchema, ALTER
sections.hook: Let intentional changes in, keep accidental ones out — and make it explicit which write may change the schema.

blocks.text: Yesterday the source had `customer_id, name, city`. Today it also has `segment`. `source_df.write.mode("append").saveAsTable(...)` **fails**.
Don't immediately enable a global setting. **First ask: is `segment` an intentional addition?** If yes, allow evolution **for this write only**:

blocks.code:
(source_df.write
   .option("mergeSchema", "true")
   .mode("append")
   .saveAsTable("prod.silver.customers"))
blocks.caption: Per-write schema evolution
Global autoMerge — not preferred for production

items.title: mergeSchema (per write)
points: Clear which write may change the schema

items.title: autoMerge (session-wide)
points: Many unrelated writes may evolve schemas
Hard to tell which operation was allowed to

blocks.text: Modern **SQL syntax** for evolution scoped to one statement:

blocks.code:
MERGE WITH SCHEMA EVOLUTION INTO target t
USING source s
ON t.id = s.id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET *
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *;

-- DBR 18.1+
INSERT WITH SCHEMA EVOLUTION INTO target
SELECT * FROM source;

blocks.title: Know both
blocks.text: For 2026 certification/real projects, know the new `WITH SCHEMA EVOLUTION` syntax **and** `.option("mergeSchema", "true")` — you'll see the latter everywhere.
**overwriteSchema is different.** It means: overwrite the data **and replace the schema/partitioning**.

blocks.code:
(df.write
   .mode("overwrite")
   .option("overwriteSchema", "true")
   .saveAsTable("ecommerce.silver.orders"))

blocks.text:
mergeSchema      -> evolve / add compatible schema changes
overwriteSchema  -> replace table schema during overwrite
**Manual evolution** — when the change is intentional, change the schema explicitly with `ALTER TABLE`:

blocks.caption: ALTER TABLE: metadata, schema and properties

blocks.title: Column mapping
blocks.text: Metadata-only **RENAME COLUMN** and **DROP COLUMN** require **column mapping** support on the table.

sections.title: Type Widening & Schema Changes Under Concurrency
sections.hook: INT → BIGINT is growth; INT → STRING is a different meaning — and every schema change is a metadata commit that can collide.

blocks.text: `quantity INT` grows so much you need `quantity BIGINT`. That is **type widening** — a move to a compatible, wider type. Delta supports it as a **table feature** (now GA).

head: From
Can widen to
blocks.caption: Supported widenings (no rewrite of underlying data files)

blocks.title: Widening ≠ arbitrary cast
blocks.text: `INT → BIGINT` is widening. `INT → STRING` or `STRING → STRUCT` are **not** — they change meaning. Type evolution does not mean 'any type to any other type'.
Supported widening changes happen **without rewriting** the underlying data files.
Now the production caveat: **schema changes are metadata changes**, and metadata changes **conflict with concurrent writes**.

11:59  production streaming pipeline running
12:00  ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMNS ...
12:00  writer fails  (MetadataChangedException)
blocks.caption: Not necessarily a bug — expected concurrency semantics

blocks.text: Databricks recommends **coordinating schema updates**: they can make concurrent writes fail and can also **stop streams** reading the table until they are restarted.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when a writer fails right after a schema change
questions: Did someone run ALTER TABLE or a schema-evolving write at that time (DESCRIBE HISTORY)?
Is the error MetadataChangedException?
Are streaming readers of this table now stopped and needing a restart?
Can schema changes be scheduled/coordinated with the pipelines that write this table?

sections.title: DESCRIBE DETAIL & Inspecting Tables
sections.hook: Three DESCRIBEs, three questions: what columns? what versions? what files?

blocks.code: DESCRIBE DETAIL ecommerce.silver.orders;

blocks.text: Returns **one row** of table-level metadata — a top debugging command.

items.def: Number of files in the current snapshot

head: Command
Answers
rows: Which versions/operations, by whom, with what metrics? (Chapter 5)
Format, location, size, number of files, partitioning, properties/features

blocks.title: Average file size
blocks.text: `sizeInBytes / numFiles` = average file size. Hundreds of thousands of files with a tiny average size → small-file pressure.

blocks.label: Think first: storage costs doubled but DESCRIBE DETAIL `sizeInBytes` didn't. Why?
blocks.text: DETAIL reports the **current snapshot**. Old unreferenced files kept for history/time travel aren't counted — check VACUUM/retention (Chapter 5).

sections.title: OPTIMIZE & the Small-File Problem
sections.hook: 10 GB in 10 files flies; 10 GB in 100,000 files crawls — same bytes, different file count.

blocks.text: Writes often produce files of 10 MB, 12 MB, 8 MB… thousands of **small Parquet files**.

head: Option
Layout
Effect
rows: Huge metadata/file-open overhead, many tiny Spark tasks, inefficient scheduling, poor scan efficiency
blocks.caption: Same 10 GB dataset

blocks.title: Look at file distribution, not just total bytes
blocks.text: Health = **number and size distribution of files**, not only total size.

blocks.code: OPTIMIZE ecommerce.silver.orders;

blocks.text: **OPTIMIZE** improves physical layout. Without clustering/Z-order semantics it does **bin packing**: compacting small files into more balanced sizes (e.g. 50,000 × 1 MB → far fewer, larger files).

A B C D E F      many small files
     │  OPTIMIZE
     ▼
   X   Y         fewer, larger files

log: REMOVE A..F, ADD X, ADD Y   (dataChange = false)
The logical data doesn't change. The `dataChange` flag in the protocol marks the commit as **rearrangement**, not a logical record change (e.g. streaming readers don't treat it as new data).

items.title: OPTIMIZE
points: Creates new files + a new version

blocks.title: Classic confusion
blocks.text: OPTIMIZE ≠ VACUUM. After OPTIMIZE, the old small files are still on storage until VACUUM removes them past retention.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when storage 'exploded'
questions: What do numFiles and sizeInBytes say in DESCRIBE DETAIL?
Is the average file size tiny (hundreds of thousands of files)?
Which writes produce so many small files (frequent small appends, streaming)?
Has OPTIMIZE run — and has VACUUM cleaned up the replaced files after retention?
Is predictive optimization enabled for this UC managed table?

sections.title: Data Skipping & File Statistics
sections.hook: The fastest file to read is the one you never open.

blocks.text: Delta stores **file-level statistics** in the log's `add` actions:

file A: customer_id min=1    max=1000
file B: customer_id min=1001 max=2000
file C: customer_id min=2001 max=3000

WHERE customer_id = 2500
  A -> cannot contain 2500 -> skip
  B -> cannot contain 2500 -> skip
  C -> may contain 2500    -> read
blocks.caption: Data skipping

blocks.text: **Data skipping** = using file statistics so files that cannot contain matching rows are not read. Stats also help pruning and query planning.

blocks.title: Skipping needs a good layout
blocks.text: If every file holds customer_ids 1…3000 (min=1, max=3000), no file can be skipped. Stats only help when values are **clustered** into narrow ranges per file.
Predictive optimization also **collects statistics** on Unity Catalog managed tables.

blocks.label: Think first: `WHERE customer_id = 1234` still scans most of the table. What could be wrong?
blocks.text: Files hold wide, overlapping customer_id ranges (bad layout/no clustering), stats missing for that column, or the filter isn't selective. Consider liquid clustering on `customer_id`.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when a selective query scans too much
questions: How is the table laid out — partitioned, clustered, or neither?
Is the table clustered on the column I filter by?
Are statistics collected for that column?
Is the filter actually selective?
Is data skipping kicking in (files read vs total files)?

sections.title: Liquid Clustering
sections.hook: Partition + ZORDER locked you in; liquid clustering lets the layout follow your queries.

items.title: Liquid clustering
points: Keys can change as query patterns change

blocks.text: Databricks describes **liquid clustering** as the layout technique that replaces traditional partitioning and ZORDER for many use cases, and recommends it for new Delta tables.

blocks.code:
ALTER TABLE ecommerce.silver.orders
CLUSTER BY (customer_id);

OPTIMIZE ecommerce.silver.orders;        -- incremental clustering
OPTIMIZE ecommerce.silver.orders FULL;   -- recluster ALL existing data

blocks.text: Setting `CLUSTER BY` doesn't rewrite old data on its own. Plain `OPTIMIZE` clusters incrementally; to apply clustering to **existing** data, run `OPTIMIZE … FULL`.

blocks.title: Why 'liquid'?
blocks.text: A static `partitionBy(country)` is concrete poured into the table's design. Liquid clustering is a shape you can change: new keys without an immediate rewrite of all historical data.

**When does it make sense?** Columns used often in **filters**, **joins** and **selective lookups**, with enough **cardinality** that physical ordering helps — e.g. `CLUSTER BY (customer_id)` when you often run `WHERE customer_id = ?`.

blocks.title: Bonus: concurrency
blocks.text: Liquid-clustered tables also benefit from row-level concurrency (Chapter 5).

blocks.title: Not combined with partitioning/ZORDER
blocks.text: Liquid clustering replaces partitioning and ZORDER on a table — you don't stack them.

sections.title: Predictive Optimization
sections.hook: Let Databricks schedule maintenance — but you still need to know why a table is slow.

blocks.text: For **Unity Catalog managed tables**, **predictive optimization** lets Databricks run maintenance automatically and decide which tables benefit.

blocks.title: Automation ≠ understanding
blocks.text: Predictive optimization does **not** mean you don't need to understand optimization. In debugging you must still know why files are small, why skipping doesn't work, why a clustering key is bad, why a scan is huge.

blocks.title: Best practice
blocks.text: Enable predictive optimization for Unity Catalog managed tables where supported.

sections.title: Production Project, Debug Workflows & Best Practices
sections.hook: Glue it all together: the e-shop pipeline, the 5 debug workflows, 13 rules and a 20-step drill.

blocks.caption: Bronze, Silver, staging

blocks.code:
MERGE INTO ecommerce.silver.orders AS t
USING ecommerce.staging.orders_updates AS s
ON t.order_id = s.order_id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET
  t.customer_id = s.customer_id,
  t.amount      = s.amount,
  t.status      = s.status,
  t.updated_at  = current_timestamp()
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT
  (order_id, customer_id, amount, status, updated_at)
VALUES
  (s.order_id, s.customer_id, s.amount, s.status, current_timestamp());
blocks.caption: Idempotent MERGE: re-running gives the same business state

head: Symptom
First command
Look for
blocks.caption: The 5 debugging workflows at a glance

blocks.title: Workflow 2 rule
blocks.text: Do **not** blindly enable `mergeSchema` — first decide whether the change is intentional evolution or a source bug.

items: Prefer Unity Catalog managed Delta tables unless you have a reason not to.
Prefer `writeTo()`/V2 semantics for modern table creation where practical.
Prefer REPLACE WHERE / REPLACE USING over legacy dynamic partition overwrite for new workloads.
Use schema enforcement as protection, not nuisance.
Enable schema evolution explicitly and locally when possible.
Use DESCRIBE HISTORY and time travel for debugging.
Do not treat time travel as long-term backup.
Prefer liquid clustering for many modern layout cases instead of static partitions.
Enable predictive optimization for UC managed tables where supported.

blocks.text: **Practical assignment** — build `ecommerce.bronze.orders_raw`, `ecommerce.staging.orders_updates`, `ecommerce.silver.orders` and do, in order:

items: Run MERGE again to prove idempotency
Add a new column with mergeSchema

blocks.text: **What's next:** Phase 3 — Unity Catalog mastery: metastore → catalog → schema → managed/external tables → volumes → credentials/external locations → grants → service principals → row filters/masks → lineage → `PERMISSION_DENIED` debugging.

debug.title: Write fails: schema mismatch
debug.symptom: Append/MERGE that worked yesterday fails today with a schema mismatch error (e.g. new column `segment`).
askYourself: What does DESCRIBE TABLE show vs df.printSchema()?
Is it a new column, a different type, or a renamed column?
Is this intentional evolution or a source bug?
If intentional, can I evolve explicitly and locally (mergeSchema / WITH SCHEMA EVOLUTION / ALTER TABLE)?
Is it a widening (INT → BIGINT) that needs type widening rather than a cast?

steps.why: New column / type / rename lead to different fixes
Don't bake source bugs into Silver
Local evolution keeps other writes protected

debug.fix: Never blindly enable mergeSchema or global autoMerge; evolve per write or via ALTER TABLE once the change is confirmed intentional.
debug.mnemonic: 3C + E: Compare, Classify, Confirm — then Evolve

debug.title: Storage exploded
debug.symptom: Storage and/or query time grew sharply; listing the table is slow.
askYourself: What do numFiles and sizeInBytes say in DESCRIBE DETAIL?
Is the average file size tiny (small-file pressure)?
Which writes produce many small files?
Has OPTIMIZE run — and VACUUM afterwards, past retention?
Is predictive optimization enabled for this UC managed table?
Is the growth actually old history files (not counted in DETAIL)?

steps.why: Let PO maintain UC managed tables

debug.fix: OPTIMIZE (or predictive optimization), VACUUM after retention, and fix writers that produce tiny files.

debug.title: Query scans too much
debug.symptom: `WHERE customer_id = 1234` still reads most of the table's files.
askYourself: How is the table laid out (partitioned, clustered, neither)?
Is it clustered on the column I filter by?
Are statistics collected for that column?
Is the filter actually selective?
Is data skipping pruning files at all?

steps.code:
ALTER TABLE ecommerce.silver.orders CLUSTER BY (customer_id);
OPTIMIZE ecommerce.silver.orders FULL;

debug.fix: Liquid clustering on the frequently filtered/joined column, then OPTIMIZE FULL; keep stats current (predictive optimization/ANALYZE).
debug.mnemonic: L-C-S-S-S: Layout, Clustering, Stats, Selectivity, Skipping

debug.title: Writer fails right after a schema change (MetadataChangedException)
debug.symptom: A streaming/batch writer fails with `MetadataChangedException` at the moment someone ran ALTER TABLE; streams reading the table stop.
askYourself: Did someone run ALTER TABLE or a schema-evolving write at that time (DESCRIBE HISTORY)?
Is the error MetadataChangedException?
Are streaming readers now stopped and needing a restart?
Can schema changes be coordinated with the pipelines that write this table?

steps.why: They must pick up the new metadata

debug.fix: Treat it as expected concurrency semantics: retry/restart, and coordinate future schema changes.

debug.title: Table lost most of its rows after a write
debug.symptom: A table with years of data now only contains the latest batch.
askYourself: Was the last write mode overwrite (DESCRIBE HISTORY → operationParameters)?
Did the DataFrame contain only a subset?
Which version was the last good one, and are its files still within retention?
Should this job use append, MERGE or REPLACE WHERE instead?

steps.why: Bring back the last good state as a new version
steps.code: RESTORE TABLE ecommerce.silver.orders TO VERSION AS OF 309;

rootCauses: Full overwrite with a subset DataFrame
debug.fix: RESTORE, then switch the job to append / MERGE / REPLACE WHERE.

debug.title: Dynamic overwrite replaced an unexpected slice
debug.symptom: After a 'one-day' dynamic overwrite, a different date's data shrank to a few rows.
askYourself: Which keys/partitions did the incoming data actually contain (SELECT DISTINCT)?
Did a stray row carry an unexpected date?
Which version changed the slice (history + time travel)?
Would REPLACE WHERE with an explicit predicate have failed safely?

steps.do: Compare versions for the damaged slice
Restore/repair and switch to REPLACE WHERE

debug.fix: Validate the incoming domain; prefer explicit REPLACE WHERE; repair with RESTORE or re-load of the slice.
debug.mnemonic: Validate the domain before you replace

debug.title: Values landed in the wrong columns
debug.symptom: After a load, `id` contains names (or numbers appear in a text column); no error was raised.
askYourself: Did I write with insertInto (positional)?
Does the DataFrame column order match the target?
Could types be coerced silently?
Which version introduced the bad rows?

steps.do: Compare DataFrame column order vs DESCRIBE TABLE
Fix code: select columns in target order or use a name-based API

debug.fix: Use name-based writers (writeTo().append(), saveAsTable append) or reorder columns explicitly.

pitfalls.title: CREATE OR REPLACE in production
pitfalls.text: Replaces definition/state of an existing table.
pitfalls.fix: Use CREATE TABLE / IF NOT EXISTS unless a rebuild is intended.

pitfalls.title: insertInto is positional
pitfalls.text: Columns matched by position; silent wrong mapping if coercible.

pitfalls.title: INSERT OVERWRITE without predicate
pitfalls.fix: Use INSERT INTO or REPLACE WHERE.

pitfalls.title: Non-idempotent writes
pitfalls.text: amount = amount + 10 or blind appends double-apply on retry.
pitfalls.fix: MERGE that sets values from a deduplicated source.

pitfalls.title: Legacy dynamic partition overwrite
pitfalls.text: Legacy, compute limitations, stray keys replace slices.
pitfalls.fix: REPLACE WHERE / REPLACE USING; validate the key domain.

pitfalls.title: Disabling enforcement mentally
pitfalls.text: Treating schema errors as a nuisance.
pitfalls.fix: Investigate: intentional evolution or source bug?

pitfalls.title: Global autoMerge
pitfalls.text: Every write in the session can evolve schemas.

pitfalls.title: Widening ≠ arbitrary cast
pitfalls.text: INT → STRING / STRING → STRUCT aren't widening.
pitfalls.fix: Use type widening only for supported wider types.

pitfalls.title: Uncoordinated schema changes
pitfalls.text: ALTER during writes → MetadataChangedException; streams stop.
pitfalls.fix: Coordinate schema changes and restart streams.

pitfalls.title: OPTIMIZE ≠ VACUUM
pitfalls.text: OPTIMIZE rewrites active files; VACUUM deletes old ones.
pitfalls.fix: Run both for their own purpose.

pitfalls.title: Judging health by total bytes
pitfalls.fix: Check numFiles and average size in DESCRIBE DETAIL.

pitfalls.title: Expecting immediate rewrite from CLUSTER BY
pitfalls.text: Changing keys doesn't recluster existing data.

pitfalls.title: Automation replaces understanding
pitfalls.text: Predictive optimization doesn't debug layouts for you.
pitfalls.fix: Still learn small files, skipping, clustering.

exercises.q: `CREATE TABLE ecommerce.bronze.orders_raw (...)` silently replaces the table if it already exists.
exercises.explain: Plain `CREATE TABLE` usually **fails** when the table exists. Replacement needs `CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE`; no-op-if-exists needs `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`.

exercises.q: In a CTAS (`CREATE TABLE … AS SELECT`), where does the table's schema come from?
options: You must declare it in parentheses first
It is derived from the SELECT query
It is copied from the source table's DDL
Delta infers it later on first read
why: Only CREATE TABLE LIKE copies a definition.
exercises.explain: CTAS derives column names and types from the query — that's why you use CAST/aliases in the SELECT to control the resulting schema.

exercises.q: Exercise 1: create an **empty** table `dev.silver.customers` with the same schema as `prod.silver.customers` — no data.
exercises.explain: `CREATE TABLE … LIKE …` copies the definition/metadata, not the rows. Great for dev/test, prod-like staging, schema cloning and migration testing.

exercises.q: In Databricks you must write `USING DELTA` or the table will be created as Parquet.
exercises.explain: Delta is the default table format on Databricks. `USING DELTA` is optional — useful only for explicitness.

exercises.q: The table already exists. What does each statement do?

items.text: CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS t (...)
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE t AS SELECT …
CREATE TABLE t AS SELECT … (CTAS without OR REPLACE)

exercises.explain: Only OR REPLACE replaces; IF NOT EXISTS skips; plain CREATE (including plain CTAS) fails on an existing table. In production, OR REPLACE must be a conscious choice.

exercises.q: CTAS: create/replace `ecommerce.silver.orders` from `ecommerce.bronze.orders_raw`, casting `order_id` to BIGINT and `amount` to DECIMAL(10,2), upper-casing `status`, keeping `customer_id` and `order_ts`.
exercises.solution:
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE ecommerce.silver.orders AS
SELECT
  CAST(order_id AS BIGINT) AS order_id,
  customer_id,
  CAST(amount AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS amount,
  UPPER(status) AS status,
  order_ts
FROM ecommerce.bronze.orders_raw;
keywords: create or replace table ecommerce.silver.orders as
exercises.explain: The SELECT defines the Silver schema; casts make types explicit instead of relying on whatever Bronze had.

exercises.q: Which statement copies data rows into the new table?
options: `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS b (id BIGINT)`
`CREATE TABLE b AS SELECT * FROM a`
exercises.explain: Only CTAS materializes query results. LIKE copies structure only; the others define an empty schema.

exercises.q: Exercise 2: target `(id BIGINT, name STRING)`; DataFrame columns `(name, id)`. Which API is the most dangerous here?
exercises.explain: `insertInto` resolves columns **by position**, so `name` goes into `id`. If types can be coerced it silently writes wrong data; otherwise it fails.

exercises.q: `df.writeTo(...)` is the DataFrameWriterV2 API, which Databricks recommends for many modern table writes.
exercises.explain: writeTo() = V2: clearer create/replace semantics, better partitioning, table properties, clustering and conditional overwrite support.

exercises.q: Match each call to its effect.
pairs: Create new table; fail if it exists
exercises.explain: V2 methods name the intent directly; the classic API encodes it in `.mode()`; insertInto is positional.

exercises.q: Target `ecommerce.silver.customers` has columns `(id, name)`. Which line causes silently swapped values?
exercises.explain: insertInto maps by position: DataFrame column 1 (`name`) → target column 1 (`id`). Either reorder to match the target, or use a name-based API.

exercises.q: Create or replace a Delta table with the V2 API.
exercises.explain: writeTo(name) → using(format) → createOrReplace(). `.create()` would fail if the table existed; `.append()` adds rows.

exercises.q: Difference between `saveAsTable(...)` and `writeTo(...)`?
options: saveAsTable is the older DataFrameWriter API; writeTo is DataFrameWriterV2 with more explicit create/replace/partitioning/table semantics
exercises.explain: Both write tables. V2 makes intent explicit (create, createOrReplace, append, overwrite…) and supports properties/clustering better; the classic API relies on `.mode()`.

exercises.q: Append `df` to `ecommerce.silver.orders` using the V2 API.
exercises.explain: V2 append is name-based and explicit. Classic equivalent: `df.write.mode('append').saveAsTable(...)`.

exercises.q: Difference between `INSERT INTO` and `INSERT OVERWRITE`?
options: INTO adds rows; OVERWRITE replaces the target scope
exercises.explain: INTO is additive. OVERWRITE replaces the target scope — without restriction, the entire table contents.

exercises.q: `TRUNCATE TABLE` removes the table object from the catalog.
exercises.explain: TRUNCATE removes rows; schema and table object remain. `DROP TABLE` removes the table object.

exercises.q: `ecommerce.silver.orders` has 1,000 rows. You run `INSERT OVERWRITE TABLE ecommerce.silver.orders SELECT * FROM staging.orders` where staging has 200 rows (no partition restriction). How many rows does the table have now?
exercises.explain: INSERT OVERWRITE replaced the whole target scope with the 200 staging rows. With `INSERT INTO` it would have been 1,200.

exercises.q: Daily batch ETL: copy today's Bronze rows into Silver.
exercises.text:
INSERT [[INTO]] ecommerce.silver.orders
[[SELECT]] order_id, customer_id, amount, status, order_ts
FROM ecommerce.bronze.orders_raw
WHERE ingestion_date = [[current_date()]];
exercises.explain: INSERT INTO … SELECT is the bread-and-butter additive load. Using OVERWRITE here would wipe all previous days.

exercises.q: TRUNCATE TABLE or DROP TABLE?

items.text: All rows removed, table still queryable
Table no longer appears in SHOW TABLES
You can INSERT into it immediately afterwards

exercises.explain: TRUNCATE empties; DROP deletes the object (and its definition).

exercises.q: Which statement does NOT keep existing rows?
exercises.explain: The first three are additive; INSERT OVERWRITE replaces the target scope.

exercises.q: When do you use append?
options: When the incoming rows are genuinely additive and don't replace existing state
When the target should exactly equal the DataFrame
exercises.explain: Append = existing + new rows, no overlap. If rows overlap or correct existing state, you need MERGE/REPLACE WHERE; 'exactly equal' is full overwrite.

exercises.q: A full overwrite is dangerous when the DataFrame contains only a subset of the table (e.g. only yesterday).
exercises.explain: Overwrite replaces the logical state with the DataFrame: 3 years of data become 1 day. One of the most classic production mistakes.

exercises.q: Order id=5 has `amount = 100`. A job runs `UPDATE orders SET amount = amount + 10 WHERE id = 5`, fails after committing, and is retried once. What is the amount now?
exercises.explain: +10 and +10 → 120. The statement is **not idempotent**: repeating it keeps changing the state. A MERGE that sets `amount = s.amount` would give the same result on every retry.

exercises.q: Idempotent (safe to re-run) or not?

items.text: MERGE setting t.status = s.status from a deduplicated source
Appending the same daily batch twice
REPLACE WHERE order_date = '2026-09-27' with the same data
Full overwrite with the same complete DataFrame

exercises.explain: Idempotent writes **set** a final state; non-idempotent ones **add to** the current state (increments, blind appends).

exercises.q: Monday morning: `ecommerce.silver.orders` (3 years of data) now holds only Sunday's orders.

options.text: DESCRIBE HISTORY to find the last write and its operationParameters (mode)
options.fb: History reveals a WRITE with mode Overwrite — the smoking gun.

options.text: Re-run all ingestion jobs for 3 years
options.fb: Slow and unnecessary while history still has the good version.
Would destroy the old files you need to recover!

steps.prompt: History: v310 = WRITE mode=Overwrite by the daily job. Recovery?

options.text: RESTORE TABLE … TO VERSION AS OF 309 (files still within retention)
options.fb: Creates v311 equal to the good state.

options.text: Time travel only — SELECT VERSION AS OF 309 fixes it
options.fb: Time travel reads; it doesn't make the state current.
Never hand-edit the log.

options.text: Change the daily job to append / MERGE / REPLACE WHERE order_date = <day>
options.fb: Never full-overwrite with a subset.

options.text: Keep overwrite but run it at night
options.fb: Timing doesn't change semantics.
Schema setting, unrelated.

exercises.explain: Overwrite with a subset = data loss in the current state. Recover with RESTORE, prevent with append/MERGE/selective overwrite.

exercises.q: What does it mean that a MERGE is idempotent, and why does it matter for production jobs?
exercises.model: Idempotent means that running the same operation again with the same input does not change the final logical state any further. A MERGE that sets target columns from a deduplicated source (e.g. id=5 → status 'PAID') gives the same table no matter how many times it runs. That matters because jobs retry after failures: a retry must not double-apply changes like `amount = amount + 10` or duplicate appended rows.
rubric: Same input re-run → same final state
exercises.explain: Mention **retries** and give a non-idempotent counter-example.

exercises.q: Daily file for 2026-09-27 may be re-delivered with corrections later that day. Which write is the best fit?
options: Selective overwrite of that day (REPLACE WHERE) or MERGE on the key
exercises.explain: Data overlap with existing rows, so plain append would duplicate; full overwrite would wipe other days. Replace that day's slice or MERGE by key — both idempotent.

exercises.q: Exercise 4: replace only `country = 'GR'` rows of `sales.orders` with `staging.orders_gr`, keeping DE/FR unchanged.
exercises.explain: REPLACE WHERE replaces exactly the rows matching the predicate and leaves everything else untouched — far safer than a full overwrite.

exercises.q: Dynamic overwrite, modern style.
exercises.explain: REPLACE USING (cols) replaces target rows whose key-column values appear in the incoming data. Recommended over legacy partitionOverwriteMode=dynamic.

exercises.q: Which pattern does Databricks recommend for selective overwrite in new workloads?
options: `REPLACE WHERE` / `REPLACE USING` (or `REPLACE ON`) depending on use case
Full overwrite then re-append old data
DELETE then INSERT in two jobs
exercises.explain: The modern INSERT … REPLACE variants are atomic and explicit. Dynamic partition overwrite is legacy with compute limitations; DELETE + INSERT in two jobs isn't atomic.

exercises.q: `.option("partitionOverwriteMode", "dynamic")` is the preferred choice for new workloads.
exercises.explain: It's legacy: still supported in some contexts, has compute limitations, and Databricks recommends REPLACE WHERE / REPLACE USING instead.

exercises.q: You ran a dynamic overwrite for 2026-09-27. Next day, analysts report that all of **2024-01-01**'s orders are gone except one row.

options.text: The incoming data contained a stray row with order_date = 2024-01-01, so that whole slice was replaced
options.fb: Dynamic overwrite replaces every key present in the incoming data.
VACUUM doesn't change the current snapshot.
Conflicts fail transactions; they don't drop rows.

options.text: DESCRIBE HISTORY + time-travel compare the 2024-01-01 slice before/after the write
options.fb: Shows the slice shrank in that exact version.
Gives current size/files, not per-slice changes.
The data evidence is in history.

options.text: Validate the incoming key domain (e.g. SELECT DISTINCT order_date) before writing, or use REPLACE WHERE with an explicit predicate
options.fb: REPLACE WHERE fails if rows violate the predicate.
Even worse.
Helps recovery, not prevention.

exercises.explain: Always validate the incoming key/partition domain; explicit predicates are safer than data-derived slices.

exercises.q: A job should only replace 2026-09-27 in a 3-year table. Which line is the bug?
exercises.fix:
(daily.write.mode("overwrite")
     .option("replaceWhere", "order_date = '2026-09-27'")
     .saveAsTable("ecommerce.silver.orders"))
# or SQL: INSERT INTO ecommerce.silver.orders REPLACE WHERE order_date = DATE'2026-09-27' SELECT ...
exercises.explain: A plain overwrite replaces the **whole** table with one day. Restrict it with a replaceWhere predicate (the DataFrame form of REPLACE WHERE).

exercises.q: Order a safe selective-overwrite routine.
items: Decide which slice to replace (e.g. order_date = 2026-09-27)
Validate the incoming key domain (SELECT DISTINCT order_date)
INSERT INTO … REPLACE WHERE <slice predicate> SELECT …
Check DESCRIBE HISTORY metrics for the new version
exercises.explain: Decide → validate → replace explicitly → verify. Validation catches stray keys before they replace unintended slices.

exercises.q: Incoming data accidentally includes one row outside the intended date. Which option protects you best?
exercises.explain: REPLACE WHERE states the slice explicitly and validates that written rows match the predicate, so the stray row makes the write fail instead of wiping another slice. Data-derived dynamic options replace whatever keys arrive.

exercises.q: What is schema enforcement?
options: Validation on write that incoming columns/types are compatible with the target schema
exercises.explain: Enforcement rejects incompatible writes (missing/unknown columns, unsafe types) using the schema stored in the log metadata.

exercises.q: Writing `amount INT` into a target column `amount BIGINT` can succeed through a safe cast.
exercises.explain: INT → BIGINT is safely castable. A complex STRUCT into BIGINT is not.

exercises.q: Default behaviour (no evolution enabled): accepted or rejected?
exercises.explain: Columns must exist and types must match or be safely castable. New columns need explicit evolution.

exercises.q: Which rules does Delta check on write? (choose all)
options: Columns must exist in the target
Types must match or be safely castable
Column order must match exactly for saveAsTable
exercises.explain: Schema validation is about column existence and type compatibility. Column order matters only for positional APIs like insertInto; row counts aren't validated.

exercises.q: Difference between schema enforcement and schema evolution?
exercises.model: Schema enforcement validates every write against the target schema and rejects incompatible data, protecting downstream tables from silent corruption. Schema evolution is a controlled, explicit change of the target schema so it can accept intentional structural changes, such as a new column, via mergeSchema, WITH SCHEMA EVOLUTION or ALTER TABLE.
exercises.explain: One protects, the other permits — explicitly.

exercises.q: Which one is NOT a goal of schema enforcement?
options: Stop a bad producer before it corrupts Silver/Gold
Reject a STRUCT arriving in a DECIMAL column
Automatically add every new column a source sends
Use the schema stored in the transaction log for validation
exercises.explain: Adding columns is evolution — opt-in and explicit. Enforcement's job is to reject.

exercises.q: Why is a global `spark.databricks.delta.schema.autoMerge.enabled = true` not the preferred production approach?
options: It lets many unrelated writes evolve schemas and hides which operation was allowed to
exercises.explain: Session-wide evolution affects every subsequent write. Per-write `mergeSchema` or `WITH SCHEMA EVOLUTION` keeps the permission local and explicit.

exercises.q: `mergeSchema` and `overwriteSchema` do the same thing.
exercises.explain: mergeSchema evolves/adds compatible changes during a write; overwriteSchema replaces the table schema (and partitioning) during an overwrite.

exercises.q: Append `source_df` to `prod.silver.customers`, allowing schema evolution for this write only.
exercises.explain: Per-write evolution: only this write may add `segment`. The rest of the session stays protected by enforcement.

exercises.q: MERGE that may evolve the schema for this operation only.
exercises.text:
MERGE [[WITH SCHEMA EVOLUTION]] INTO target t
USING source s
ON t.id = s.id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET *
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *;
exercises.explain: `MERGE WITH SCHEMA EVOLUTION INTO` scopes evolution to that statement — the SQL counterpart of per-write mergeSchema.

exercises.q: A notebook fixing a failing append. Which line is the anti-pattern?
exercises.explain: The global setting also lets `other_df`'s write (and every later one) evolve schemas silently. Scope evolution to the one write that needs it — after confirming the new column is intentional.

exercises.q: Today's append to `prod.silver.customers` fails with a schema mismatch. Yesterday it worked.

options.fb: See exactly which column/type differs.
Blindly evolving can bake a source bug into Silver.

options.text: Drop the target and recreate it from the DataFrame
options.fb: Destroys data and history.

steps.prompt: The DataFrame has a new column `segment STRING`. Next question?

options.text: Is `segment` an intentional addition, or a source bug?
options.fb: Intentional evolution vs bug is the key decision.
Irrelevant to schema.

options.text: How many files does the table have?
options.fb: Irrelevant here.

options.text: Per-write .option('mergeSchema','true') (or ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMNS segment STRING)
options.fb: Local, explicit evolution.

options.text: Set autoMerge globally for the cluster
options.fb: Too broad: unrelated writes could evolve too.
overwriteSchema replaces schema on overwrite — wrong tool.

exercises.explain: DESCRIBE TABLE vs printSchema → new column/type/rename? → intentional? → explicit local evolution. Never blind mergeSchema.

exercises.q: Match each tool to its effect.
pairs: Evolve schema for all writes in the session
SQL insert that may evolve schema (DBR 18.1+)
exercises.explain: Know the scope of each: per write, per session, replace, manual DDL, per SQL statement.

exercises.q: Manual evolution on `prod.silver.customers`: add `email STRING`, then rename `name` to `full_name`.
exercises.solution:
ALTER TABLE prod.silver.customers ADD COLUMNS (email STRING);
ALTER TABLE prod.silver.customers RENAME COLUMN name TO full_name;
exercises.explain: ALTER TABLE makes intentional changes explicit. Metadata-only rename (and drop) requires column mapping on the table.

exercises.q: Metadata-only `RENAME COLUMN` and `DROP COLUMN` on Delta require column mapping support.
exercises.explain: Without column mapping, Delta identifies columns by name in the Parquet files, so renames/drops can't be metadata-only.

exercises.q: Which statement needs DBR 18.1+ according to the course?
exercises.explain: INSERT WITH SCHEMA EVOLUTION is the newest form (DBR 18.1+). MERGE WITH SCHEMA EVOLUTION, mergeSchema and ALTER have been around longer.

exercises.q: What is type widening?
options: Any type change, e.g. INT → STRING
A compatible move to a wider type, e.g. INT → BIGINT or FLOAT → DOUBLE, without rewriting data files for supported cases
exercises.explain: Widening keeps meaning and only expands range/precision. INT → STRING changes semantics and isn't widening.

exercises.q: `STRING → STRUCT` is a supported type widening.
exercises.explain: Widening ≠ arbitrary cast. STRING → STRUCT changes the data's meaning entirely; type evolution doesn't mean 'any type to any type'.

exercises.q: Enable type widening on `ecommerce.silver.orders` and widen `quantity` to BIGINT.
exercises.explain: Type widening is a table feature: enable it, then widen. Supported changes don't rewrite the underlying Parquet files.

exercises.q: Supported widening or not?
exercises.explain: Widening goes to a wider compatible numeric type. Narrowing (BIGINT → INT) loses range; INT → STRING / STRING → STRUCT change meaning.

exercises.q: 12:00 — a streaming pipeline writing to `prod.silver.orders` fails with `MetadataChangedException`. At 12:00 a colleague ran `ALTER TABLE prod.silver.orders ADD COLUMNS (channel STRING)`.

options.text: No — schema changes are metadata commits that conflict with concurrent writes
options.fb: Expected optimistic-concurrency semantics.
Concurrency exceptions prevent corruption.
It does; it just reacts to schema changes.

options.text: Streams reading the table may stop until restarted
options.fb: Schema changes can halt streaming readers too.
Nothing like that happens.
The ALTER committed fine.

options.text: Coordinate schema changes with pipeline owners (maintenance window), then restart affected streams
options.fb: Databricks recommends coordinating schema updates.

options.text: Disable the transaction log during ALTERs
options.fb: Not a thing.

options.text: Enable autoMerge globally so ALTERs aren't needed
options.fb: Trades a coordination problem for uncontrolled evolution.

exercises.explain: Schema change = metadata change → conflicts with concurrent writers and can stop streams. Coordinate it.

exercises.q: Supported type-widening changes rewrite all the table's Parquet files.
exercises.explain: Supported widening is metadata-level: the underlying data files are not rewritten — readers upcast values on read.

exercises.q: Order the steps to widen `quantity` from INT to BIGINT safely in production.
items: Coordinate the change with pipelines writing the table
ALTER TABLE … ALTER COLUMN quantity TYPE BIGINT
Restart streams that read the table if they stopped
exercises.explain: Schema changes are metadata commits that conflict with concurrent writes — coordinate first, enable the feature, widen, then restart affected streams.

exercises.q: What does `DESCRIBE DETAIL` show?
options: Current table-level metadata: format, location, numFiles, sizeInBytes, partitioning, properties/features
exercises.explain: DETAIL = one row of current table metadata. Versions → DESCRIBE HISTORY; columns → DESCRIBE TABLE.

exercises.q: Which command answers which question?
pairs: What schema does my DataFrame have?
exercises.explain: Schema-mismatch debugging pairs DESCRIBE TABLE with printSchema; storage debugging uses DETAIL; data-change debugging uses HISTORY.

exercises.q: DESCRIBE DETAIL shows `sizeInBytes` = 20 GB and `numFiles` = 200,000. What's the average file size in **KB**? (use 1 GB = 1,000,000 KB)
exercises.explain: 20,000,000 KB / 200,000 = 100 KB per file — classic small-file pressure. Healthy Delta files are typically in the hundreds of MB to ~1 GB range.

exercises.q: `DESCRIBE DETAIL` returns one row with table-level metadata.
exercises.explain: One row: format, location, size, numFiles, partition/clustering columns, properties, features…

exercises.q: Which field does NOT come from DESCRIBE DETAIL?
exercises.explain: operationMetrics is per-version info from DESCRIBE HISTORY.

exercises.q: Cloud bill for the table's storage doubled, but `DESCRIBE DETAIL` `sizeInBytes` stayed flat. Most likely explanation?
options: DETAIL measures the current snapshot; old unreferenced files (history) aren't counted — check VACUUM/retention
exercises.explain: Removed files still occupy storage until VACUUM. DETAIL reports the current snapshot only, so history-driven storage growth is invisible there.

exercises.q: What is the small-file problem?
options: Files under 1 GB can't be read
Too many small physical files create metadata, file-open and task-scheduling overhead
exercises.explain: Total bytes may be fine; the number of files kills performance: listing, metadata, many tiny tasks, poor scan efficiency.

exercises.q: OPTIMIZE physically deletes old unreferenced files from storage.
exercises.explain: OPTIMIZE rewrites active files into a better layout (new version). Deleting old unreferenced files is VACUUM's job, after retention.

exercises.q: A 10 GB dataset is stored as files of 100 KB each. How many files is that? (1 GB = 1,000,000 KB)
exercises.explain: 10,000,000 KB / 100 KB = 100,000 files — option B from the lesson, versus 10 × 1 GB in option A. Same bytes, vastly more overhead.

exercises.q: Without clustering/Z-order, what does `OPTIMIZE` do?
options: Bin packing: compacts small files into more balanced, larger files
Sorts all data by primary key
exercises.explain: Plain OPTIMIZE = bin packing. With liquid clustering it also organizes data by the clustering keys.

exercises.q: OPTIMIZE or VACUUM?
exercises.explain: OPTIMIZE = layout/performance; VACUUM = physical cleanup. Often run together: OPTIMIZE, then later VACUUM removes the replaced small files.

exercises.q: `ecommerce.silver.orders` storage and query times exploded after a streaming job went live.

options.fb: numFiles and sizeInBytes reveal file count and average size.
Useful later, but file counts come from DETAIL.
Dangerous and doesn't fix layout.

options.text: Small-file pressure from frequent tiny writes
options.fb: Hundreds of thousands of tiny files = classic small-file problem.
Skew is uneven partition sizes, not tiny files.
Unrelated.

options.text: Run OPTIMIZE (or enable predictive optimization), then VACUUM after retention to drop replaced files
options.fb: Compaction + later cleanup.
VACUUM doesn't compact active files.
Doesn't change file layout.

exercises.explain: DETAIL → numFiles/sizeInBytes → small files → OPTIMIZE (+ predictive optimization) and VACUUM later.

exercises.q: After OPTIMIZE, the commit can use `dataChange = false` because the data was rearranged, not logically changed.
exercises.explain: The protocol's dataChange flag distinguishes rearrangement (compaction) from real record changes — e.g. so streaming readers don't reprocess compacted files as new data.

exercises.q: Stats: file A customer_id 1–1000, file B 1001–2000, file C 2001–3000. Query: `WHERE customer_id = 2500`. How many files must be read?
exercises.explain: Only C's min/max range can contain 2500. A and B are skipped without being opened — that's data skipping.

exercises.q: What is data skipping?
options: Using file statistics so files that cannot contain matching rows are not read
exercises.explain: Min/max (and null count) stats per file let the engine prove a file can't match the predicate.

exercises.q: Which file-level statistics does Delta typically store? (choose all)
exercises.explain: These stats live in the add actions and drive pruning, skipping and planning. Query latency is not file metadata.

exercises.q: If every file contains customer_ids from 1 to 3000, min/max statistics can still skip most files for `customer_id = 2500`.
exercises.explain: Each file's range [1, 3000] contains 2500, so no file can be skipped. Skipping needs a layout where values are clustered into narrow per-file ranges.

exercises.q: `SELECT * FROM ecommerce.silver.orders WHERE customer_id = 1234` still scans most of the table.

options.text: Table layout and clustering: is data organized by customer_id?
options.fb: Without clustering, every file spans many customers.
Scan volume isn't a memory setting.
Unrelated.

steps.prompt: Layout: partitioned by order_date, no clustering. Stats exist but every file spans the full customer_id range. Also check?

options.text: Filter selectivity and whether data skipping actually prunes files
options.fb: Confirms skipping is ineffective due to layout.
VACUUM doesn't affect current file ranges.
Unrelated.

options.text: Consider liquid clustering on customer_id, then OPTIMIZE (FULL for existing data)
options.fb: Clusters values into narrow ranges so skipping works.
Scans the same data faster but more expensively.
High-cardinality partitioning creates huge numbers of tiny partitions — liquid clustering is the modern answer.

exercises.explain: Layout → clustering → stats → selectivity → skipping. Liquid clustering on the filter column is often the fix.

exercises.q: Explain why data skipping can fail even though Delta collects min/max statistics.
exercises.model: Statistics only help if each file holds a narrow range of the filtered column. If data was written in arrival order, every file may contain nearly the full range of customer_id, so for any value every file's min/max range overlaps and nothing can be skipped. Missing statistics for that column or a non-selective filter also defeat skipping. Clustering the data on the filter column fixes the ranges.
rubric: Stats help only with narrow per-file ranges
exercises.explain: Link stats to physical layout.

exercises.q: Why is liquid clustering different from static partitioning?
options: Clustering keys can evolve without immediately redesigning/rewriting the historical layout, and clustering is applied incrementally
It requires ZORDER on every column
It only works on external tables
exercises.explain: Partitioning is a fixed physical design; liquid clustering is adaptable and incremental.

exercises.q: Cluster the orders table by customer and recluster existing data.
exercises.explain: ALTER … CLUSTER BY sets the keys; OPTIMIZE … FULL applies clustering to all existing data (plain OPTIMIZE clusters incrementally).

exercises.q: Running `ALTER TABLE … CLUSTER BY (customer_id)` immediately rewrites all historical data.
exercises.explain: Changing keys doesn't force an immediate rewrite. New writes/OPTIMIZE apply clustering incrementally; OPTIMIZE FULL reclusters everything.

exercises.q: Which column is the best liquid-clustering candidate for an orders table queried mostly with `WHERE customer_id = ?` and joined to customers?
exercises.explain: Good keys are used in filters/joins/selective lookups and have enough cardinality for layout to help. status has too few values; never-filtered columns don't help.

exercises.q: Which is NOT a typical reason to choose a clustering key?
exercises.explain: Very low cardinality gives physical ordering little to work with.

exercises.q: Assignment steps 18–19: enable clustering on `ecommerce.silver.orders` by `customer_id`, then cluster all existing data.
exercises.solution:
ALTER TABLE ecommerce.silver.orders CLUSTER BY (customer_id);
OPTIMIZE ecommerce.silver.orders FULL;
exercises.explain: CLUSTER BY sets keys; OPTIMIZE FULL rewrites existing data accordingly. Afterwards compare DESCRIBE HISTORY/DETAIL.

exercises.q: Which statements about liquid clustering are true? (choose all)
options: Databricks recommends it for many new Delta tables instead of partitioning + ZORDER
Clustering keys can change as query patterns change
Liquid-clustered tables also use row-level concurrency
You should combine it with partitionBy on the same keys for best results
exercises.explain: Liquid clustering replaces partitioning/ZORDER rather than stacking on top of them.

exercises.q: Which maintenance operations can predictive optimization run automatically? (choose all)
exercises.explain: PO handles maintenance: compaction/clustering, cleanup, statistics. RESTORE and MERGE are data operations you decide.

exercises.q: With predictive optimization enabled you no longer need to understand optimization.
exercises.explain: Automation doesn't replace engineering understanding: you still debug small files, failed skipping, bad clustering keys and huge scans.

exercises.q: Predictive optimization is recommended for which tables?
exercises.explain: Databricks recommends PO for UC managed tables — it monitors and maintains them, and also collects statistics.

exercises.q: Manual maintenance or predictive optimization?

items.text: Collects statistics on UC managed tables

exercises.explain: PO turns calendar-driven maintenance into need-driven maintenance.

exercises.q: A teammate says: "We enabled predictive optimization, so performance tuning is solved." Respond.
exercises.model: Predictive optimization automates maintenance on UC managed tables — it runs OPTIMIZE, VACUUM and ANALYZE when it judges they help. But it doesn't choose the right clustering keys for our queries, doesn't fix a pipeline that writes millions of tiny files, and doesn't explain why a query scans everything. We still need to understand small files, data skipping, statistics and layout to debug and design tables.
rubric: PO = automated OPTIMIZE/VACUUM/ANALYZE on UC managed tables
Examples: clustering keys, small files, skipping, huge scans
exercises.explain: Balance: appreciate automation, keep ownership.

exercises.q: Match each debugging workflow to its first command.
pairs: MERGE fails: multiple source rows matched
exercises.explain: Five workflows, five entry points. Memorize the pairs — they are the first 30 seconds of every Delta incident.

exercises.q: Which is NOT one of the Phase 2 best practices?
options: Enable schema evolution explicitly and locally
Use time travel as long-term backup
Prefer liquid clustering over static partitions for many cases
exercises.explain: Rule 10 says the opposite: do NOT treat time travel as long-term backup.

exercises.q: Order the first part of the practical assignment.
items: Run MERGE again to prove idempotency
exercises.explain: Steps 1–9: build up writes, DML, then break and fix MERGE and prove idempotency.

exercises.q: Order the second part of the practical assignment.
items: Add a new column with mergeSchema
exercises.explain: Steps 10–20: schema evolution, inspection, time travel/restore, then small files → OPTIMIZE → clustering → OPTIMIZE FULL.

exercises.q: Best practice or anti-pattern?

items.text: Blind full overwrite with a daily DataFrame
Prefer REPLACE WHERE / REPLACE USING over dynamic partition overwrite
Global autoMerge for the whole cluster
Enable predictive optimization on UC managed tables

exercises.explain: The 13 rules reduce to: explicit, local, idempotent, and let the platform maintain layout — while you understand it.

exercises.q: Write the project's idempotent MERGE: target `ecommerce.silver.orders`, source `ecommerce.staging.orders_updates` on `order_id`; on match set customer_id, amount, status, `updated_at = current_timestamp()`; otherwise insert those columns.
exercises.solution:
MERGE INTO ecommerce.silver.orders AS t
USING ecommerce.staging.orders_updates AS s
ON t.order_id = s.order_id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET
  t.customer_id = s.customer_id,
  t.amount = s.amount,
  t.status = s.status,
  t.updated_at = current_timestamp()
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (order_id, customer_id, amount, status, updated_at)
VALUES (s.order_id, s.customer_id, s.amount, s.status, current_timestamp());
exercises.explain: It **sets** values from the source, so re-running yields the same business state (only `updated_at` refreshes). That's what makes retries safe.

exercises.q: Order the schema-mismatch workflow.
items: Classify: new column / different type / rename
Decide: intentional evolution or source bug?
Evolve explicitly (mergeSchema / ALTER) or fix the source
exercises.explain: Workflow 2. The decision point is 'intentional or bug?' — never blindly enable mergeSchema.

exercises.q: In the 'someone broke data' workflow, RESTORE comes before DESCRIBE HISTORY.
exercises.explain: History first (find the bad version), time travel to confirm the last good one, then RESTORE if needed.

exercises.q: Why does the project MERGE count as idempotent even though it sets `updated_at = current_timestamp()`?
options: Business columns are set from the source, so re-runs converge to the same logical state; only the audit timestamp refreshes
MERGE is always idempotent regardless of SET expressions
exercises.explain: Idempotency is about the final logical/business state. An audit timestamp changing is acceptable; `amount = amount + 10` would not be. A MERGE with increments is not idempotent.

exercises.q: According to the course, `REPLACE WHERE` is supported on all compute types, while legacy dynamic partition overwrite has compute limitations.
exercises.explain: One more reason to prefer REPLACE WHERE / REPLACE USING for new workloads: no compute-type restrictions, explicit semantics, atomic replacement.

exercises.q: Overwrite the table AND replace its schema (deliberately).
exercises.explain: overwriteSchema only makes sense with overwrite mode: it replaces data and schema/partitioning. To just add a column during append, use mergeSchema instead.

exercises.q: Goal: append today's rows and accept the new `segment` column. Which line is wrong?
exercises.explain: overwrite + overwriteSchema replaces the whole table (data and schema) with today's rows. Appending with an extra column needs mode append + mergeSchema.

exercises.q: Goal: cluster the existing orders by customer_id. Which line won't do what the comment claims?
lines: -- now ALL historical data is clustered by customer_id
exercises.fix:
ALTER TABLE ecommerce.silver.orders CLUSTER BY (customer_id);
OPTIMIZE ecommerce.silver.orders FULL;  -- recluster existing data
exercises.explain: Setting CLUSTER BY doesn't rewrite historical data. Run OPTIMIZE … FULL to apply clustering to all existing records (plain OPTIMIZE is incremental).

exercises.q: Storage debugging: fill in the command and the two fields you read first.
exercises.explain: DESCRIBE DETAIL gives one row of table-level metadata; numFiles and sizeInBytes reveal small-file pressure (average file size).

exercises.q: Compact small files.
exercises.explain: OPTIMIZE bin-packs small files into larger ones (and clusters if keys are set). VACUUM would only delete old unreferenced files.

exercises.q: After yesterday's load, `ecommerce.silver.customers.id` contains values like 'Maria' cast weirdly / NULLs, and `name` contains numbers. No job failed.

options.text: The load used a positional writer (insertInto) with a different column order
options.fb: Silent swaps without errors are the signature of positional resolution.
Enforcement checks types/columns, not intended mapping by position.
VACUUM doesn't change current data.

options.text: Use df.writeTo(target).append() (name-based) or select columns in target order
options.fb: Removes the positional dependency.
Schema evolution doesn't fix mapping.
Would wipe the table and still swap columns.

steps.prompt: And the bad rows already written?

options.text: Find the bad version in DESCRIBE HISTORY and RESTORE (or repair) it
options.fb: History pinpoints the load; RESTORE repairs.
Silent corruption propagates to Gold.
Never hand-edit the log.

exercises.explain: Positional writes swap columns silently when types can be coerced. Use name-based APIs.

exercises.q: Values landed in the wrong columns. Order the investigation.
items: Check whether the writer used insertInto (positional)
Compare DataFrame column order with DESCRIBE TABLE
Fix code: name-based API or reorder columns
RESTORE or repair the version that introduced bad rows
exercises.explain: Identify the positional API, prove the order mismatch, fix the code, then repair the data.

exercises.q: A table lost years of rows after a daily job. Order your response.
items: DESCRIBE HISTORY: find the WRITE with mode Overwrite
Confirm the DataFrame contained only a subset
RESTORE the last good version (within retention)
Change the job to append / MERGE / REPLACE WHERE
exercises.explain: Locate, confirm, recover, prevent.

exercises.q: A writer fails with MetadataChangedException right after an ALTER TABLE. Order the response.
items: DESCRIBE HISTORY: find the concurrent ALTER / schema-evolving write
Restart the failed writer and any stopped streams
Agree a coordination process for future schema changes
exercises.explain: It's expected concurrency semantics: identify the change, restart, and coordinate next time.

exercises.q: Storage exploded. Order the workflow.
items: DESCRIBE DETAIL: read numFiles and sizeInBytes
VACUUM after retention to remove replaced files
exercises.explain: Measure, diagnose small-file pressure, find the cause, compact, then clean up.

exercises.q: A selective query scans too much. Order the checks.
exercises.explain: Workflow 4: layout → clustering → stats → selectivity → skipping; often the fix is liquid clustering on the filter column.
